utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have the accused brought in, Mr. Registrar. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First of all, would I like to say good afternoon to the interpreters, and to everybody else as well, to make sure everybody can hear, the Prosecutor, the Defence, and then we can resume our work. We'll work today until 6.15, since we didn't begin before 2.15. We'll work until 6.15. Let me check our permanent clock, the registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let's have the witness brought in. Mr. Katava. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Your Honours. Just as we're waiting for the witness to settle, may I introduce Patricia Reynders who will be our case manager. A new face in the courtroom. She will be our case manager for the foreseeable future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We'll say good afternoon to Patricia Reynders. I'm sure she speaks French perfectly. Thank you for your answer. We want to welcome her very heartily to this courtroom. Mr. Katava, do you feel all right. Did you rest up a bit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Mr. Cayley, I suppose you didn't sleep a wink last night. You have files in your mind, files in front you, briefs, but we're going to look at the real clock now, turning to the registrar. Let's say it's 2.30, so you have about, I say about, about, a half hour for your cross-examination about all of the documents, and the Defence will have the same amount of time for its redirect. So without any further ado, we can begin now. All right. Mr. Cayley, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, you said about a half an hour. I think you meant about an hour. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I know your sense of humour, Mr. Cayley. I do note that the translators had also such a good sense of humour and would also distort my words. No, it's an hour, an hour. I said approximately an hour, because we're not going to count every second.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Katava.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your examination-in-chief you said that in '92 and '93, 1992 and 1993, the police force in Busovaca was poorly equipped and organised. Would that be a fair summary of what you stated?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said that they worked within the scope of their possibilities, the material and technical equipment they had available. I did not say that they were equipped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. Your answer's fine, Mr. Katava. Now, five years has passed, and peace has come and the Federation police force has been formed. Would you say that the police force in Busovaca has improved during that time in terms of its quality?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Well, now we have conditions that are a bit better, so we work a bit better too. Also we've been rather successful in structuring the police, and there is training too, Your Honours, so the police force is of a different quality now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say that things are better now than they were in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993 there was a war on and now it's peacetime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if the witness can have placed in front of him Exhibit 450. Defence Exhibit 450. Now, Mr. Katava, you're familiar with the documents contained in this file?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you select these documents, sir, for the purposes of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: No, I didn't, Your Honour. This is only part of the documents that were put forth to me by the lawyers. There are more documents on this. These are documents related to the way in which we worked then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I'm right in saying that Mr. Nobilo selected the documents that are in that file?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I don't know who selected the documents. I had a look at them though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you -- although you're familiar with those documents, you have no idea upon what basis they were selected for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've just stated that these documents are only part of the documents that were put forth by you to the lawyer. How many more documents are there other than these that are contained in this file?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My learned colleague is twisting the witness's words. The witness did not say that he had put forth the documents to me, but that he had seen these documents with the Defence. So it's not this witness that put them forth to me. He didn't bring any documents to me at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to consult my colleagues on a point. Mr. Cayley, the Judges were concerned about the -- about your not overly interfering in the relationships between the witness and his counsel. You can ask for some information, but you should always be concerned about the code of ethics. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, did you yourself select the pool of documents from which the documents contained in this file were selected?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I did not make a selection of any documents. I simply corroborated the authenticity of the documents that I had seen. Among these documents are some that I had personally drafted, but I did not select them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there many more documents similar to these at the Busovaca police station?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Probably. Notes similar to these.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those notes would fall into the same categories as are listed in A to K on this index. In fact, A to G, because that's all we're dealing with today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, probably, because we took note of everything we did. These documents are more or less the same like these, made according to the same principle, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have just stated that, in fact, a number of the documents in this selection were drafted by you. Now, for how many years have you worked at the Busovaca police station?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not set aside these documents. I simply said that among these documents are some that I had personally drafted, but I did not distinguish between the documents in any way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, I asked you how many years you'd served in the Busovaca police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: From 1977 I have been working in the Busovaca police station. For three years before that I worked in the Teslic police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are very familiar with the way documents are drafted at the police station, with your over 20 years of experience?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with the way in which these documents are drafted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we can turn to document 13, which I think is a document that you drafted. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you'll see underneath the title of the document there is a file number. Can you explain to the Judges how the file numbering system worked at the Busovaca police station?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I think that this is the protocol of the Busovaca police station. This is an official note, and it was registered, and it concerns a certain event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And every official document that was drafted at the police station had a protocol number like this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I don't know whether every one of them had one, but every official document is supposed to have a protocol number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So every official document that was drafted at the police station had a file number; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I cannot claim that every document had one, Your Honour, I can only speak of the documents I see in front of me, but it is customary practice in any institution to have file numbers. That is as much as I know about protocols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you yourself, of course, worked in the police station for more than 20 years; didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that time it was customary, it was practice, for all official documents to have file numbers attached to them, wasn't it, Mr. Katava?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes. For as long as the system functioned, that's the way we did it. We, the policemen, wrote our notes and the protocol was then taken care of by other people, because I would simply draft a report, and then I would give this to my superiors who would then deal with the protocol. I didn't interfere with the protocol. Our job was to submit the documents that we would write to our superior officers and that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Katava. Now, if we can turn to tab F, section F. Now, I think these are statements of Muslims desiring to leave Busovaca; is that correct? Mr. Katava, is this the section that deals with the statements of Muslims desiring to leave Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Please allow me, Your Honours, to have a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, that is the section that speaks of the voluntary departures and stating the reasons why they were leaving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that accords with the index which is in English at the front of this exhibit. Now let us look at Exhibit 36. Now, this, I think, which is again part of this section on the statements of Muslims desiring to leave Busovaca, is a statement taken from a Muslim soldier summoned to the Busovaca police station and asked a number of questions about the conflict in January of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document is a statement made by a friend of mine, the one I mentioned yesterday. He came of his own free will and said what he did. He said that his wife and children went to Kacuni and that he stayed there, and that he is prepared to co-operate. That's the only thing it says, nothing else. I mean, we did not question him. He came to the station of his own free will, and he gave this statement to my colleague. I personally know the gentlemen who made this statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this statement generally concerns a Muslim soldier speaking to the authorities about his role in the conflict in January, does it not, Mr. Katava?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: He came on his own and he said what he wanted to say, and my colleagues simply wrote this down and that is what is in this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, you're not answering my question. My question is this: This statement is describing the role of a Muslim soldier in the conflict in January; isn't it? It has nothing to do with that man's voluntary departure from the municipality of Busovaca. The Judges have the statement in front of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes. This man came voluntarily and explained the role he had in Busovaca at that time. Nobody forced him to do it. And all this information was written down by my colleague and entered in this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to document 37. Now, this, I think, is a document where five Muslim males -- I think they're males but certainly five Muslims -- are asking for approval from the police station in Busovaca to leave the municipality on a voluntary basis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This document states that we had a regular practice to take statements from people who wished to leave Busovaca voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, why was it necessary for people who were volunteering to leave the municipality to seek your approval?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: We had instructions to protect people, to see whether someone was mistreating them, to see whether somebody was forcing them to leave. For those reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But why was it necessary for an individual who wished to leave of their own free will to obtain a permit to leave the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Asked and answered, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps the answer was not complete. Mr. Cayley, you can continue with the question. It's a relevant question. Go ahead, Mr. Cayley. Mr. Katava, try to answer. Why would somebody of his own free will ask for authorisation to leave the city? Mr. Hayman, did you want to say something further?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, he answered the question point-blank, straight on, and for the question to be repeated and for the Court to admonish him is serious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I was set on English and not French. I did not understand the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, you give us the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, I won't give the answer, Your Honour, but I can state what the witness stated. Mr. Cayley said: Why would it be necessary for a person to come to the police station to get a permit who wanted to leave the municipality? The witness said: We were instructed to do so, to interact with these people, because it was our job to protect them and make sure they weren't being forced to leave. So by regulating the departure of people, it was an effort, according to the witness, to make sure they weren't being intimidated, threatened, and forced to leave. He has answered the question in a very poignant and pointed way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, by speaking too long, you begin to dictate the answers that you might prefer to hear the witness say. I have to ensure balance in these proceedings. Mr. Cayley, take into account the answer that you have been given, but you can go on with the same theme; that is, to know how or why, in a free city, people could not come in or go out normally? I think this would be of interest to the Judges. It is true that I don't want you to ask the question exactly in the same way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Katava, we'll move on to mistreatment of people within the municipality. Simply this: Why was it necessary for an individual who wished to leave of their own free will to obtain a permit from the police station so to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Your Honours, at that time, checkpoints had been set up. There was a curfew in order to prevent crime, and we had instructions that we talk to these people, question them, and see why they were leaving Busovaca; and with their permits, they could then go across these checkpoints if they expressed the desire to leave, but only once we had ascertained that nobody had forced them to leave or had mistreated them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was it necessary for them to hand their keys over to the police, the keys to their houses?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: No, this was not compulsory for everybody. Those who left from other people's houses would leave those keys which would be handed over to the centre for social work and for the refugees, the refugee centres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at Exhibit 37 where it states in respect to five individuals leaving. When they were leaving, they brought the keys to their houses to the police station and handed them in. Why were those keys handed in to the police station, Mr. Katava?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: In this document, Your Honours, you can see that these are refugees from Jajce, Doboj, Rogatica, so they were taken in in Busovaca and accommodated in other people's houses. Once they left Busovaca, it would be normal for them to return the keys because the houses weren't their property, and they went of their own free will to join up with their families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at documents 38 and 39, Mr. Katava. Now, document 38 is again a statement, an official note being made by a Muslim leaving Busovaca who is required to make an affirmative statement that he's neither being mistreated by the police or by any citizens in Busovaca. Were Muslims mistreated by the police in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. From this document, one can see that statements were not taken -- this is just a note taken by the policeman when he questioned this particular individual, and from these notes, you can see that I myself was present, and that when the man put forward his reasons, we allowed him to leave Busovaca with his family, and my own name is mentioned in this document. So we did not mistreat anybody. I personally never mistreated anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was it necessary for an individual to make an affirmative statement that they had not been mistreated by the police, Mr. Katava?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: This is official notes or records, Your Honour, made by a policeman written on the basis of the talk he had with the individual in question mentioned in the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, again, you're not answering my question. Why was it necessary for an individual Muslim leaving Busovaca to make an affirmative statement that they had not been mistreated by the police?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that I have answered. We did not insist that people make affirmative statements saying that the police did not mistreat them. This was just an observation made by the particular policeman saying that the man had left of his own free will and that he had not been mistreated by anybody, and that is the statement, what the man told the policeman, and the policeman made his own notes and wrote them down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to document 39, Mr. Katava. Now, again, I think in this statement, it states in the first paragraph: "I remained in the house where I also did not have any problems such as harassment by the local inhabitants of Busovaca or the police." So the same phrase is in this official note as well, isn't it, Mr. Katava?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Just one moment, please, Your Honour, for me to read the statement, if I may?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last sentence, first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: This document was also drawn up by the same policeman as the one a moment ago and probably this is the form in which he wrote these official documents, and this is a statement in this case, the statement that the individual gave to the policeman who was my colleague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Muslims were mistreated by the police, weren't they, Mr. Katava, in Busovaca, and that's why it was necessary in these documents for these people to state that they were not being mistreated by the police? That was required for them to be able to leave, wasn't it, Mr. Katava?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, my learned colleague is not asking questions, he is entering into a discussion of opinions with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cayley, Mr. Nobilo is right. Ask your question, but make a comment at another time. Ask the question, ask it clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to document 40, Mr. Katava, and here I think if you look in the second paragraph, you'll find that it states: "I had no problems when the fighting broke out or afterwards and was not mistreated by members of the HVO."

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: What is your question, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the previous three documents, Mr. Katava, we have seen that every single Muslim who wanted to leave had to state that they were not either being mistreated by the HVO or by the police. It was a standard requirement, wasn't it, Mr. Katava, that Muslims had to make that declaration before they could leave Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: It was not a requirement, Your Honour. We had this standard practice, to ask them for protection purposes, why they were leaving, had they been mistreated, had they been beaten, had they been thrown out and mistreated? So in this statement, it clearly states the reasons why this individual is leaving Busovaca with his family because he has a family living outside Busovaca and wants to join up with that part of his family. Nobody mistreated these individuals or forced them to make statements of this kind. Quite simply, people asked to leave, and you know what it's like in a war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Katava, if a Muslim wanted to enter the municipality of Busovaca from outside, did they also require permission or a permit from the police?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: At that time, they had to go to the police and say why they had come, state why they had come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that document 41 is, in fact, an example of that, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: May I have a few minutes to look through it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, this is an official note made by my colleague, the policeman, from which we can see that Mr. Muminovic, with his wife, had come to Busovaca during the cease-fire and that he was brought by a neighbour, Milinovic, a Croat. That is what is noted in this document, nothing else. That is to say, that the man had returned from Vitez to Busovaca with his wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document also notes that he had returned without a previous approval or entry permit issued by the Busovaca police station, doesn't it, Mr. Katava?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: It means that Mr. Muminovic did not report to the police station, and the policeman took note of the fact that he did not come to the police station but went home, and he went home because a friend, Mr. Milinovic, had brought him home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If an individual arrived in Busovaca without approval or an entry permit, would they be summoned to the police station in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: They would not, Your Honours, because the police has its own method of work. The policeman in the field would ascertain why the man had come. He would talk to him. He would get information as to why the person had arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at document 42 in which an individual arrived in Busovaca without a permit and who was, in fact, you'll see, at the top of this document, summoned to appear at the police station. Now, this man was summoned, wasn't he, to the Busovaca police station, because he didn't have a permit to be living in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, this individual was not summoned. We are dealing with two people here who were arrested by the police during the curfew and taken to the police station. So it was curfew. They were moving around during the curfew, two unknown individuals, and they were taken to the police station at Busovaca, and this is the statement which says that they were taken to the police station during the curfew hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to document 43, Mr. Katava. Now, this document concerns two individuals who had come to visit relatives in Busovaca, two individuals, and they needed a permit even whilst on a visit simply to get out of Busovaca again, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: May I read through the document, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I don't have to tell you each time, Mr. Katava, but every time you want to read one, of course, you can, before you answer any of the Prosecutor's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an individual who wished to return to Busovaca because they did not have the means of livelihood here. It is a refugee from Jajce, and his wife and children were in Janjici near Zenica, and he had gone to Busovaca to get the means for a livelihood. He entered Busovaca during the curfew, and that is what this document states, that he entered Busovaca while the curfew was in force, and I think that that is what the document states.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're looking at the wrong document, Mr. Katava. It's document 43. I think you are looking at document 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Forty-three?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forty-three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Forty-three. I have number 43.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mine may be misnumbered. Document 43, does it begin: "Compiled on 29 March, 1993 on the premises of the Busovaca police station"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it begins, and it is about Mr. Cazim Arnautovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's document 42. I think if you turn to your next document ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: The number I have is 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, I have the same numbering system as you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. What I have is Cazim Arnautovic number 42, whereas Senad Dindic is 43. Senad Dindic is 43. And you should have the same. So the note is "Compiled on 29 March, '93" for Senad Dindic. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it, but I have number 42. It's numbered as 42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It was number 42 and now it is 43 in my copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think everybody else, Judge Riad, has 43 apart from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise. There seems to be an error by my associates compiling this file. I would now like to say that Senad Dindic is 43 and Cazim Arnautovic would be 42. So that the minority can put this right. So Senad Dindic was 43 and Cazim Arnautovic was 42 and the date is the same. The official notes were written on the same date. Probably that is why the error occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, have you had the opportunity to read document 43?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I'll just take a few minutes to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Forty-three after the correction?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Judge. I think your file was correct. I think it was only the witness's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You want Senad Dindic or --

utterances.speaker: MR. REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Dindic is 43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you finished Mr. Katava?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. These are two persons, Esad Kalauzovic and Senad Dindic. It is obvious from this document as well that these two persons were moving around during the curfew, and, therefore, they were brought into the police station. As they were brought in, they expressed a wish to leave Busovaca, with their families, and all of that can be seen from this document. So they were moving around during the curfew and they were brought into the station, these two persons, Esad -- sorry Senad Dindic and Esad Kalauzovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Katava, these two individuals came to Busovaca, and 12 people left; didn't they? Ten members of their family left with them after they'd been to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Your Honour, it says here, literally, as they expressed the wish to leave with their -- to take their families to Zenica, this wish of theirs was granted and then they left. This is probably a mistake; they left on the 29th with their families. They could not leave without their families when they were in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But these two individuals had come from outside the Busovaca municipality, Mr. Katava, to Busovaca initially; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: These individuals, and it says so here very nicely, Your Honours, it says that they were moving around during the curfew. They and their families were staying in Busovaca, and after that they asked to leave Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your testimony is that these two Muslim males were walking around during curfew hours, they were collected by the police, taken to the police station, and then suddenly just decided to leave Busovaca with their families? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Your Honours, I repeat what this document says. This document was written by a colleague of mine, a policeman, and it says here, literally, that they were brought in by the police after they were asked for their IDs, and the reason for this was they were walking around during curfew hours. Also, that a conversation was carried out with them afterwards why they were walking around during curfew hours, and they said they had come to see their relatives who were staying in the house of Bitic Ramiza, to see them there, to see their relatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it goes on to say, Mr. Katava, that after the interview, in your presence and the presence of Nikica Petrovic, these two gentlemen asked for a permit enabling them and their families to leave Busovaca municipality. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says here, Your Honour, that after the conversation they asked to leave Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next document, which is document 44. Now, this, I think, is a document where this gentlemen asked three times to voluntarily leave Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Do you please repeat the number once again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Document 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Your Honours, Faik Kresevljak is number 44 and this pertains to another person. This man is from Busovaca. I know him personally, Faik Kresevljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did this gentlemen have to ask three times to voluntarily leave Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I personally know Faik, this individual. This is a person whose mental health is not all that great, and you will see, Your Honours, that he and his wife kept coming to the police all the time, because it was great fun for them to come to the police. They lived on their own, they had nothing else to do, and they had something to report all the time. Why he said this, that is his own personal affair, but what he said was also reported in this statement. I mean, I think that finally this individual did leave the municipality of Busovaca of his own free will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think the final document, document 45, is, again, a Muslim being required to have a permit to re-enter the municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes. This document also speaks of a lady whom I know. Before the conflict she left Busovaca. She went to the area of Vitez, and at this time she returned to Busovaca. She returned during curfew hours, and that is why the police interviewed her. And she made a statement to the police that she came on foot via a certain checkpoint, and you can't see anything else from here. She returned during curfew hours, and she made a statement to the police that she came on foot from Vitez to Busovaca, and that before the conflict she went to Vitez, and this is to say that she returned at this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read to you the third paragraph: "Because of the curfew and restrictions on movement, the above named has asked, on a number of occasions, to be allowed to return to Busovaca, and since a permit is needed both to enter and leave Busovaca, on 29 March, 1993 she arrived in Busovaca without the necessary entry permit." Now, my question is this: It was the requirement for Muslims to have a permit from the police to either leave or enter the municipality, wasn't it, Mr. Katava?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. This is to say that everybody needed a permit to move around during curfew hours. Everybody had to have a permit in order to be allowed to walk around during curfew hours. This is not a gentlemen, this is a lady Enisa Merdan. I know her personally. It says here that she left Busovaca before the conflict. She went to Vitez, and then she came back via this checkpoint on foot, which she told my colleagues. So no one is allowed to move around during curfew hours without a specific permit. This is police work, and one knows who is allowed to move around during curfew hours. It did not pertain only to Muslims, it pertained to all citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at this document, in the final paragraph, Mr. Katava, you'll find that she, in fact, arrived at 2.00 in the afternoon on the 29th of March, 1993. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that curfew hour, 2.00 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. All the time. The curfew was on for 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your testimony to the Court is there was a 24-hour curfew? Nobody at all was allowed out on the streets without a permit from the police?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: For reasons of safety and security. We've already taken care of this. We've said this before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So am I correct in saying that anybody, Muslim or Croat, needed permission from the police in Busovaca to be moving about in the street at any time of the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: During the curfew one had to have a permit, and when it is not curfew hours --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, what were the hours of curfew?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the people who reached this decision on curfew hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've just stated to the Court that curfew was 24 hours a day. Was it not 24 hours a day?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: During one period of time it was, Your Honours, but I cannot remember exactly which period this was, but probably it was that period. If it says here that it was during curfew hours, then it was during curfew hours, because I trust the colleague who wrote this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your testimony is that at 2.00 on the 29th of March, 1993, this woman was travelling during curfew hours and that's why she needed a permit to re-enter Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not asserting that, Your Honour. I'm simply stating what this document says. My colleague said that this person was moving about during curfew hours and that is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where does it say in the final paragraph that she arrived during curfew hours, Mr. Katava?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: In the last paragraph, Your Honours, it says that she arrived on foot, that she had hitchhiked, she stopped a vehicle that was going towards Busovaca, and then from the checkpoint at Sunce she continued, went on foot and entered Busovaca. As she entered Busovaca, she did not have any problems because probably people knew her. I mean, the persons manning the checkpoint at Sunce probably knew her and allowed her to go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It doesn't say anything about a curfew, does it, Mr. Katava, at 2.00 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: In the last paragraph, no mention is made of the curfew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, all of these documents in section F --

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, but there's something wrong with the volume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, is your headset working satisfactorily now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, all of these documents, from 36 to 45, do you recall, earlier in your testimony, you stated it was customary for documents to have a protocol number? You will find that not one of these documents has a protocol number. Have those numbers been removed, Mr. Katava?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. You saw the document that I had personally drafted. As an experienced policeman, I wrote a certain protocol number which I knew from earlier on, and this document was done by a colleague of mine who did not take care of the protocol. He simply left a space for the number and the date. This was done by my colleague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier in your testimony, Mr. Katava, that you didn't insert the protocol numbers, that it was done by your superiors. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: No. I said, Your Honours, that we had the following practice in the police, and this practice prevails to the present day, that the policeman writes a document and submits it to his superior officer, and the policeman did not take care of the protocol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from documents 36 to 45, on each of these occasions the police officer forgot to insert a file number. If you can find a file number on any of these documents, Mr. Katava, I would be very interested, because it means you have a different set than me. Are there any file numbers on any of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I did not understand the question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you indicate, on any of the documents between 36 and 45, whether any of those documents have a file number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: No, not here. It only states the date. Also, there is a space left for the protocol. But the documents are authentic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated earlier that it was standard practice to insert a protocol number, didn't you, Mr. Katava?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I said that from my experience as a policeman, Your Honours, that before it was the prevailing practice, but this was wartime, and I put a number on one of these documents because I tried to be a smart guy, because I've been a policeman for so long. But the other documents were done by my colleagues, and they simply didn't do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we've established, have we not, Mr. Katava, that Muslim and Croats needed a permit from your police station to either enter or exit the town of Busovaca during curfew hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit 456/12. Now, while you're waiting for that document, Mr. Katava, am I right in saying that your police station in Busovaca answered to the police station in Travnik? Travnik was the regional police station?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. To the police department in Travnik. The police department in Travnik, during the conflict, was removed to Vitez and its headquarters was in Travnik. So it was called the police department Travnik, located in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you will see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Would you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is an order from the then Colonel Blaskic to allow people to return to their homes, and it's a joint order, you can see, signed by Colonel Blaskic and signed by Enver Hadzihasanovic. Do you see, in paragraph 3, that it states that unimpeded and safe movement be ensured for the whole population throughout the free territory? The order is dated the 13th of February, 1993. It's a command, it's an order, and the Travnik police department is on that command. Now, Mr. Katava, why were you requiring Muslims to obtain permits to leave and enter Busovaca if an order had been issued by Hadzihuseinovic and Colonel Blaskic to allow the free and unimpeded movement of the population throughout the area of the Central Bosnian Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't answer this. I was a plain policeman. I did not make any decisions. I simply carried out the duties that were given to me. I can't really comment on this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, did you know, at the time when you were issuing these permits to Muslims, that they were supposed to be allowed to move freely throughout the territory in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Well, it was precisely with the intention of ensuring their free movement that we talked to them and gave them permits to leave, or to come back or whatever at their initiative, because they requested us to do this for them for the purposes of their own security, and we tried to protect them from mistreatment, assaults by individuals and criminal groups, et cetera. So it was the same reason. We did not want to restrict their freedom of movement, because there could not be freedom of movement if there were checkpoints. Civilians had to be cautious. They had to know when they would move around, when they would cross these checkpoints, because there was always a danger of them being wounded. The frontline was nearby. It's a very small area, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your testimony to the Judges is that by seeking permission -- by Muslims seeking permission to exit or enter Busovaca, this was a means of actually ensuring the free movement of the population throughout Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Among other things, it was the right way for a person to go from Busovaca to Zenica safely, because the frontline was in between. If one crossed the frontline on his own, one could get killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move to section C of these documents. Now, documents 27 to 31 concern damage to the mosque in Busovaca in the period from September of 1993 to May of 1994. Mr. Katava, what was the month of 1993 in which you first started investigating damage to the mosque?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Your Honours, in document 27, this is an eyewitness statement, and I immediately started investigations concerning this matter. The mosque was looted, and one can see here that it was the loudspeakers and the rugs, the Hodza were taken away. We worked on this particular matter, and this is an eyewitness statement that I had personally written. It also says that -- that I carried out the investigation in the presence of the Hodza and the head of the Islamic community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was first done in September of 1993; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes. This happened during -- between the 1st and 2nd of September, 1993, and I was there. I carried out the investigation, and I made this file and this file probably still exists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you investigate damage to the mosque in February of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I cannot recall and there is not a document of this nature here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Judges in this court have heard testimony that as early as February of 1993 the mosque in Busovaca had been damaged. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you investigate damage to any other Muslim religious sites, structures or buildings in the municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: No. This is the only building belonging to the Islamic community that was destroyed -- damaged during the war in Busovaca. Everything else remained intact. The monuments, everything else. It is only this building that was damaged during the war, and there are documents relating to that here too. But the fact remains that we worked, that we intervened, and that we took care of it and that we carried out inspections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many police officers were working at the Busovaca police station in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Your Honours, most of the policemen were engaged in defence, and there were three or four of us there, regular police officers there. I said this yesterday. We had various teams for carrying out investigations on the site. There were some 20 of us doing all the different duties, whereas the other policemen were engaged on the frontlines, defence lines, and they were defending.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we can now move to section E of the file, and I've been advised by Mr. Nobilo that we'll move into closed session at this time. Mr. President, if we could have a closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We agree, but I should like to indicate the time. We had overstepped the one hour limit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But the Judges have consulted with one another. We consider that these are important points. We will leave Mr. Cayley the time he needs, but if you go over the time it won't be counted against you, Mr. Nobilo. Would you like to take a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I mean, Mr. President, I understand the point my learned friend is making, and I will try and move as quickly as possible. I don't think it's going to take another hour, but it is more than I originally anticipated. I apologise to the Court for that. It may now be an appropriate time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We're going to take a break and then we'll have a closed session for tab E, and we will respect the rules of balance here, and the Defence will have an equal amount of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing now. Have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We can resume now. I think that there was a request from the Defence for a closed session. Is that all right with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just have actually one question, one or two questions before that, and then we can move into a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Ask them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the break, Mr. Katava, we were speaking of curfew hours. Are you aware of the individual who set the curfew hours in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: No, I'm not. I don't know who ordered the curfew.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 507?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will see this is an order dated the 7th of January, 1993, to HVO Central Bosnian Operative Zone brigades, HVO municipal authorities, and the Vitez Regional Military Police, and it's to supplement an order of the 5th of December and it's an order from Colonel Blaskic. Now, paragraph 1 concerns the opening hours of hotel and catering establishments, and paragraph 2, if you look at paragraph 2, it states the curfew hours. Paragraph 2(c): "The curfew hours are, in the municipalities of Busovaca, Kiseljak, Kresovo, Vares, Kakanj, and Zenica are from 2300 hours, 11.00 at night, until 4.00 in the morning.".

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes. We can see that. That is so from this order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when Enisa Merdan was moving through a checkpoint at 2.00 in the afternoon in March of 1993, there were no curfew hours in force, were there, Mr. Katava?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: You're probably right, Your Honours, but we had to see who was coming in and going out for security reasons, and citizens were duty-bound to report to the police station, and anybody who wished to leave had to say he was leaving. A citizen coming in to Busovaca in normal times still is duty-bound to report to the police station and say that he is residing there, and in these extraordinary times, this was even more necessary, the exits and entrances for safety reasons. So it might not have been a curfew, but we had to know who was entering Busovaca because this was a time of war, because spies could have come or the enemy could have come. So for our own personal safety, we had to know who was moving around the town, and it is normal procedure, standard practice, when you move around from town to town and take up residence, to go to the police station and tell them of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was not true what you stated before, that the reason this woman required a permit was because she was moving around in curfew hours? That's not correct, is it? In fact, it was for different reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear what reasons. The question isn't clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, it is not a two-edged question, it's a logical question. The Prosecution counsel is asking how you can explain the reasons that in document whatever number its number is, there was a person about whom you said that she had not obeyed the curfew rules at 2.00 in the afternoon. Now you are being asked whether you are being consistent with your initial answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Mrs. Enisa Merdan had come via the checkpoint on foot and she was allowed to enter the town, and my colleague talked to her and she said that she had come to Busovaca and had not asked for any permit to do so, and he questioned her with regard to the circumstances under which she arrived in Busovaca, and he noted that Mrs. Enisa Merdan had come to Busovaca and was at present located in Busovaca, nothing more than that. And that when passing the checkpoints, she had no problems from the policemen or anybody else. They probably knew her, they knew that she was an inhabitant of Busovaca and so let her pass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the break, Mr. Katava, you said that this woman, Enisa Merdan, had entered Busovaca during curfew hours. Why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I did not say that in that way. I said that that is what is written in the note from my colleague, that she was moving around during curfew. I did not say that she entered during curfew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, let's not [interpretation cut off]. There was no mention of curfews being there. It's a question of logic, you see. Either you're changing your explanation, which is your right. I think it's a question of logic. You've got to go back to the transcript. Give your version and then move to another question, and the Judges can make their own evaluation, but let's not change the version that you're giving constantly. That's what we mean. Yes, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I propose that we place the document in front of Mr. Katava again, the document on the arrival; and second, Mr. Katava, on the first occasion and now, always said the same thing. He said "I think it was a curfew," and that is why my colleague wrote it down in his notes. He didn't say he knew it was a curfew. He said that sometimes a curfew would last for 24 hours and at other times for shorter periods. So he has, in fact, changed nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Your objection is not accepted, Mr. Nobilo. Mr. Cayley, continue asking questions in that area until the witness gives testimony which is consistent with what he has said up to this point. Mr. Katava, you're working with professional Judges who are listening to what you have to say. Try to be logical. Let me remind you that the task in which the right to require a certain coherence on the part of the witnesses and some witnesses have to recall that, remind some of the witnesses of that. You can say what you like, but there must be a degree of logic in what you're saying. Mr. Cayley, go ahead. Go ahead in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, previously, prior to the break, you stated that Enisa Merdan arrived in Busovaca in March of 1993 during a curfew hour at 2.00 in the afternoon. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said that that is what is written in the official note of my colleague, a policeman, that Enisa Merdan had arrived at that time, because that is what is written in the note, in the document, and I am just conveying what was written in the note. I was not present when Mrs. Enisa Merdan came. This was observed by my colleague, the policeman, in his note.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now your testimony is that the reason she needed a permit was because of security reasons rather than the curfew?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not say that she needed a permit to move around. A permit during curfew is something that the Croats and Muslims need alike, and Mrs. Enisa Merdan came, and my colleague observed, in an official note, that she had come, that he had talked to her regarding the circumstances of her arrival in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're now saying that Mrs. Enisa Merdan did not, in fact, need a permit to move around either to or from Busovaca; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: You cannot move around during a curfew; then you need a permit to do so. The individual did not seek a permit but she came on foot across the checkpoint and nobody stopped her, and then my colleague talked to her when she came home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Mr. Katava, this was at 2.00 in the afternoon. There was no curfew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I did not say that there was a curfew. I said that in the note written by my colleague, that that is what was stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the transcript will speak for itself on this matter. I'll move on. If we could have a closed session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We'll move into closed session. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Public session then. (Open session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you turn to section A of your file, please, Mr. Katava? Again, I'm going to, first of all, ask you about a document that you drafted, which is document 6. Do you see the signature in the bottom right-hand corner? Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this document have a file number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you signed it, did it have a file number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I do not recall, but, Your Honours, there didn't have to be a file number every time. It was a war situation. It is the contents of this document that are important. I think that we've been dealing with this number too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Judges will decide how much time should be spent examining a document, Mr. Katava. This is not the first time that we've run into numbering problems, Mr. Katava, it's not the first time that we've had numbering problems in documents, and I want to say that the Judges will evaluate all of the materials having to do with the credibility of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to put something on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The allegation that is being made here by Mr. Cayley, that this witness fabricated documents and that these documents, one can infer or suggest they're fabricated because no protocol number has been filled in to the blank that has been left for them, we deem very serious, very grave. We will suspend the Defence case for any evidence they have that any one of these documents is fictitious. These documents are full of names, persons who were interviewed, statements that they gave on certain dates. If there is one witness they can produce suggesting that one of these documents is not authentic, we will suspend the Defence case and allow the Prosecutor to put that evidence on today, tomorrow, a week from Monday, whenever. It's very serious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: -- and we will give our time, if the Prosecutor has the evidence to back up the innuendo that he has been engaging in ad nauseam today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I would like to ask you to calm down, please. I myself, the Presiding Judge of this Trial Chamber, allowed myself to say two things to the witness. First of all, that we were the ones who decide about the time that we would devote to reviewing evidence. Let me remind you of that. At the same time, I explained myself to the witness in order to give him an explanation of the time that we devote to examining documents, because it's true, this is not the first time, as you know, and the witness knows it as well, that we had a significant problem with identifying documents, starting with documents which -- for which you gave explanations, and which also had to do with another incident which was raised with the Registry about conditions under which certain documents had been provided to the translation service. That's what I wanted to say. As regards the allegations -- let me finish. Let me speak about the allegations when you say you would suspend the presentation of your case. Mr. Hayman, you, of course, are free to adopt whatever strategy you like. I consider that this incident is closed, and Mr. Cayley is entitled to ask questions, and for the time being he has asserted nothing, he's merely asking questions about numbering. I would like to express the Judges' concern about having numbered document. That's what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I am simply noting that in a public forum, to accuse a police officer of 25 years with fabricating documents is a serious and grave allegation, and it should not be allowed to stand in the public arena any longer than is absolutely necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There was no allegations about falsification. Let me remind you of that. That was not an assertion. The Prosecutor simply said -- but let me remind you that your own witness, Mr. Hayman, said, if my memory doesn't fail me, your own witness said that his colleagues could sometimes forget to put in the protocol number, but he would never forget because he was a professional policeman. Personally, I can understand, as a Judge, I commit myself here, that I ask myself the very question, but it's your witness who said it. We can go back to the transcript. He said, "As a professional policeman, when I drafted reports I never forgot to put in a number." Let's not turn things upside down. Let's close the incident with that. Mr. Cayley, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Katava, if you look at documents 6 to 12, you will find that, again, none of these documents have any file numbers on them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, on a few documents there is a file number and my signature, which is identical. Let me put it this way: I did put a number on some, and I got have forgotten in other cases. You can also see here there is the number and -- the protocol number I put in myself in some places and in other places it is not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just confirm that on documents 6 to 12 there are no protocol numbers, and also on documents 17 and 18 there are no protocol numbers, they're missing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question, Mr. Cayley. Would you repeat it, please? Perhaps it was interpretive. Could you confirm that documents 17 and 18 didn't have -- 12 didn't have numbers. No, I see it here. All right. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says here, but on two of my documents there is a protocol number. Sometimes I would put one in and sometimes I wouldn't. It depended on the situation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now talk about the content of some of these documents. I don't have time to go through all of them with you, but document 6 is a case in which you were directly involved. Do you have document 6 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think, in summary, this involved the assault of a 63-year-old woman, a probable rape of that same woman, from the comments that you recorded in the statement, and theft of property from her house. Would that be an accurate summary of what took place?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I personally know this elderly lady, and I helped her after this incident. She was assaulted, and you can see from here that she was assaulted and that she was robbed by criminals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think she identified two men in uniform as responsible for the incident. If you look, I think it says on the third line, in fact, in yours it's on the fourth line, "Two armed men in uniform."

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It says that at 00.30 hours, that a grey vehicle came up and the two uniformed men walked out who were armed. That is what it says here, because I took a statement from her with regard to the situation, with a view to the further investigation that would be carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, arrest the suspects in the course of your further investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: No, no. The perpetrators remained unknown and the file was sent to the Prosecutor, and the file remained with an unknown perpetrator. That's the only thing we could have done. We took care of the lady and we helped her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these two individuals were in uniform. Did you conclude at the time that they might have been members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Well, at that time almost everybody wore a uniform. Those were probably criminals who had carried out this robbery and attacked this old woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you inform anybody in the HVO military authorities that this incident had taken place?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, we did have a co-operation with the local Military Police, and we informed them about this event too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they conduct further investigations?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, they did conduct further investigations. That was the agreement. We worked as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they find out, the Military Police, after their further investigations?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I don't know what they found out, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know whether they arrested anybody or charged anybody in respect of this incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what the military policemen undertook, because they are the Military Police. I'm a civilian policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the civilian police did not identify any suspects in connection with this crime that took place?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: No, we did not, Your Honours, but we did record the case and took a statement from the lady, because it was a criminal act and we wrote a report in order to disclose -- uncover the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at document 8, Mr. Katava. Again, if you're reasonably familiar with this document, I think. This is a recorded statement in which a gentleman by the name of Pero Arapovic is identified as having stolen a tractor from Atif Barucija. Is that correct, as far as you can recall, from this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This statement was taken by my colleague, as he did in many cases. We can see from it that the individual did steal the tractor from Atif Barucija. "Atif Barucija." It was not correctly pronounced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies for my pronunciation. I think Mr. Barucija was told, on the 9th of March, 1993, to come and collect that tractor from the HVO Military Police who identified it and took it to Busovaca; wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We can see that the Military Police went to the house of the individual who had stolen the tractor, and that they took him to the Military Police, and they told the other man to come and fetch his tractor. This was something that was done by the Military Police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then if you read at the end of the report it states, and this is the individual who made the statement, Mr. Barucija, states, "The next day I went to the Military Police and was received by Malenica, who told me that he had been informed by the appropriation of my tractor, that the tractor had been taken away somewhere and would be returned to me as soon as they found it."

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it states, and this was done by the military policemen. I think that they returned the tractor in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did they return the tractor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I think they returned the tractor at that time, that the tractor was returned, because they knew who stole it and disciplinary action was taken against this individual. And I can't meddle into the affairs of the Military Police. This is the statement that was given by the individual when he contacted him, and he was told to wait, and as soon as the tractor turned up the tractor would be returned to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, the statement says very clearly that the Military Police had appropriated the tractor for their own use; doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot comment on the conduct of the Military Police in this case. I don't know that they confiscated it. I don't have any information on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it normal procedure for the HVO Military Police to retain stolen property?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Normal procedure, in my opinion, is for something that has been stolen to be taken away and then to be returned to the rightful owner, and to take steps against the perpetrator, the person who had stolen it in the first place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you stated that Mr. Pero Arapovic, the original thief, was charged and prosecuted. What was the punishment that he received?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I said that disciplinary measures were taken against him by the Military Police. We did not work with Pero Arapovic. And I said that it is written here they identified Pero Arpovic as the thief of the tractor, and that they took the tractor away from him. That is to say, the Military Police took the tractor away from him because he had stolen it, and it would be normal, in my opinion, to return the tractor with a receipt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What disciplinary action was taken against Mr. Arapovic for this theft?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I don't know what disciplinary action was taken by the Military Police and the military policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to document 13. Now, this is an offence of robbery, and you will see from the official note which was compiled by you that an individual by the name of Oreskic, a member of the HVO, was identified as being involved in this offence. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, I can see this. The document was one that I compiled. This individual is a displaced person from Kotor Varos, and we identified him as the thief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I'm right in saying that you informed the HVO Military Police about this incident, and that, I think, is document 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that is the document by which we informed the Military Police that the individual in question had carried out a theft in the house of a Muslim Sevala Beslic and Seval Siljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you interview Oreskic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: We only identified the perpetrator and handed the whole case over, the Oreskic case, to the Military Police, because we did not have the right to charge members of the HVO. This young man was a member of the HVO and he had carried out a robbery, and so it was up to the Military Police to take the matter further, but we identified the perpetrator of the robbery, and it was our duty to inform the Military Police to take the man over. I don't know what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was a serious case, Mr. Katava. Didn't you follow up on what the HVO Military Police did about this incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I have already told you we identified the perpetrator and handed over our report to the Military Police as to who did it, and that is where our work stopped. Our competency ceased there. It was our duty to identify the robber and then to inform the competent institutions which would then take over the case, and I think that this document -- with this document we completed our duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever follow-up on any cases in which you'd been involved to see whether people were charged or tried by a court, or given a punishment or a sentence? Did you ever follow-up on any of the cases in which you were involved?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Your Honours, other people deal with analysis and analytics. I'm an operative man, I'm a policeman working in the field, and at that time I tried to discover who the perpetrators were, to identify the criminals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So the witness is being consistent, Mr. Cayley. He worked in civilian police matters, and he simply transmitted things to other authorities. Move to another question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we look at document number 16, please, Mr. Katava? I think this is another case in which you were involved. Again, this is an illegal entry into a house and an assault on a female Muslim by the name of Sevala Beslic, and the individual involved was identified as Mr. Vinko Puljic, a member of the HVO Military Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. At the end I make this observation, and I complied this note, and by operative means the officers arrived at information that these individuals used passenger vehicles of a cream colour, and that one of these individuals, Vinko Puljic, was a member of the Military Police. So once again, by operational means, we arrived at these facts and Vinko Puljic could have been one of the perpetrators of this crime, and we also informed the Military Police thereof. But as I say, we were operative officers working in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so, again, you have no idea what the HVO authorities did about this incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: I only said that cases of this kind we handed on further to the Military Police, because the Military Police is in charge of its members. But we did name and identify the individual who could have been the perpetrator of this particular crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Katava, it would be fair to say, in respect of documents 1 to 18, you have no knowledge about whether or not any further action was ever taken against any of the persons that were identified as potential perpetrators of criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: MR. KATAVA (continued)
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is logical to my mind that if somebody is charged and that -- I think that the institutions of the Military Police probably did take disciplinary measures. Now, what the Prosecutor did after that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
